newsitem.title: CZECH REPUBLIC: Czech Senate run-off divides governing coalition.
newsitem.headline: Czech Senate run-off divides governing coalition.

text.p: Deep cracks opened on Tuesday in the three-party Czech ruling coalition -- the longest-serving post-Communist government in Europe.
At issue is a sharp dispute over supporting each others' candidates in run-off elections to the new Senate this weekend.

Prime Minister Vaclav Klaus, who leads the senior Civic Democratic Party (ODS), called the refusal of the heads of the two junior parties in the centre-right coalition to give blanket support to ODS candidates "scandalous".
"I...regard it as scandalous that we did not manage to find a common voice..," he told a news conference.

The coalition Christian Democratic Union (KDU-CSL) and Civic Democratic Aliance (ODA) both said -- after ODS put 76 candidates in second-round runoffs out of 81 constiutencies -- it was up to local party leaders to endorse whom they wanted.

Both KDU-CSL chairman Josef Lux and ODA chief Jan Kalvoda, each a vice-premier, criticised Klaus and his party for directly appealing to unsuccessful first round candidates from each party to back ODS candidates in the second round.
Lux criticised Klaus for contacting individual candidates personally and going over the heads of the coalition parties' leadership in Prague.
"Everyone is learning democracy, including the prime minister," Lux told a rally in the Czech capital on Tuesday.
The Czech agency CTK quoted Kalvoda as saying Klaus "violated political culture" through his tactics.
The three-party conservative coalition, dominated by ODS, has had a series of internal spats since forming in 1992.

ODS candidates won three seats outright in last weekend's first round by getting more than 50 percent of the vote in their constituency, and 73 candidates took the most votes in their district going into the run-off.

The strongest opposition party, the Social Democrats, who took away the coalition's majority in the lower house with a better than expected result in June elections, put only 48 candidates in the Senate runoffs, and won no seats outright.

The centre-left Social Democrats have said they would rather their supporters, in districts where they did not have a candidate in the run-off on Friday and Saturday, backed any candidate other than those from the ODS.
